implementation_notes: C99 designated initializers are the closest thing C has to named arguments: one struct holds every setting, callers fill it by member name (`struct server_cfg cfg = { .port = 9000 };`) and omitted members are zero-initialized - which is why a library that wants non-zero defaults ships a `*_default()` starter that installs them. Compound literals extend the struct form to ad-hoc calls, and the legacy alternative is a key-tagged setter table (`lib_set_int(h, LIB_OPT_TIMEOUT_MS, 5000)`, as curl and nng do it) applied to an initialized handle in call order. The function-per-option structure of the pattern is hand-written in C and only worth keeping when options must change a live object; for construction, prefer the struct.
pitfalls: Omitted designated fields are zero-initialized, not set to the library's intended defaults; without a `*_default()` starter, `{.timeout_ms = 0}` silently means 'no timeout' rather than 'library default'.

Compound literal lifetime: taking the address of a compound literal creates an object with automatic storage that dies at the end of the enclosing block, so storing that pointer in the long-lived object leaves a dangling pointer.
Duplicate designators are legal and the last one wins, so generated or macro-composed initializers silently override a setting instead of reporting a conflict.

The struct layout is the ABI: adding a member changes sizeof and can break binary compatibility, and designated initializers only protect source compatibility while the struct definition is visible to callers.

variants.name: Key-tagged option setter table (curl and nng style)
variants.implementation_notes: Libraries with a long-lived handle expose one setter per value type plus an enum of option keys (`curl_easy_setopt(h, CURLOPT_TIMEOUT_MS, 5000L)`, `nng_socket_set_ms(...)`): the handle is created with defaults, options are applied in call order and each call reports its own status. This predates C99, keeps the option set open to later additions without changing a struct's layout, and suits settings that must change after construction - at the cost of no compile-time check that all settings were supplied and no single place where the whole configuration is visible.
pitfalls: Each setter returns a status that is easy to ignore; unchecked setters leave the handle silently misconfigured.
Settings are applied imperatively after construction, so a partially configured handle exists between calls and must not be used by another thread yet.
Option keys and value types are linked only by convention (an enum plus typed setters), so a wrong key/value pairing is a runtime error rather than a compile error.

variants.name: Variadic macro over a compound literal (keyword-argument trick)
variants.implementation_notes: A variadic macro wraps a compound literal so the call site spells keywords: `#define server_start(...) server_start_(&(struct server_cfg){ .host = "localhost", .port = 8080, __VA_ARGS__ })`. Omitted members keep the macro's defaults and a repeated designator overwrites the earlier one (last wins), so the trick gives C keyword arguments with defaults at the cost of macros, preprocessor diagnostics and no checking of option names beyond struct members. It is a real technique (21st Century C, and later blog posts) but fragile enough that C libraries usually prefer the plain struct plus a defaults starter.
variants.code_sketch:
#define server_start(...) \
    server_start_(&(struct server_cfg){ .host = "localhost", .port = 8080, __VA_ARGS__ })

server_start(.port = 9000);             /* host keeps the macro default */
server_start(.port = 9000, .port = 1);  /* last designator wins: 1 */
pitfalls: Option names are checked only against the struct members; a misspelled designator is a compile error only while the struct is visible, and macro expansion errors point into the macro rather than the call.
Defaults are duplicated in the macro and in the library, so the two copies drift and conflicting options cannot be detected.
The compound literal's lifetime is the enclosing block, so the API must copy the configuration before returning.
